final.content:
# The State of Deepfake Detection Research Since 2022

## 1. Introduction

Since 2022, deepfake technology has evolved from a niche research concern into a mainstream societal threat, accelerated by the release of consumer-grade tools based on generative adversarial networks (GANs), diffusion models (e.g., Stable Diffusion), and modern text-to-speech / voice-conversion systems (e.g., ElevenLabs). Between 2023 and 2024, the number of deepfakes detected in fraud cases rose approximately fourfold, and an estimated 500,000 deepfakes were shared on social media in 2023 alone (Chandra et al., 2025; https://arxiv.org/html/2503.02857v4). This report synthesizes recent research on detection methods, cross-domain generalization, transformer-based and foundation-model approaches, multimodal and privacy-preserving techniques, the benchmark-to-deployment gap, ethics, and the regulatory response.

---

## 2. Technical Methods for Video Deepfake Detection

### 2.1 CNN and Transformer Architectures

Through 2022–2024, detection architectures have shifted from pure CNN backbones (Xception, EfficientNet, ResNet) toward Vision Transformer (ViT)–based and hybrid designs. A 2024 systematic review analyzing studies on FaceForensics++, DFDC, and Celeb-DF reported that transformer-based architectures exhibit approximately 11.33% cross-dataset performance decline, compared with more than 15% decline for CNN-based approaches, though at 3–5× higher computational cost (https://www.mdpi.com/2673-2688/7/2/68).

The "A Timely Survey on Vision Transformer for Deepfake Detection" (Khan et al., 2024; https://arxiv.org/html/2405.08463) catalogued 14 ViT-based detectors. Notable results include:

- UIA-ViT (2022): AUC of 99.33 on FaceForensics++ (HQ); cross-dataset AUC of 94.68 (DFD), 82.41 (Celeb-DF-v2), 86.59 (Celeb-DF-v1), 75.80 (DFDC).
- ISTVT (2023): 99.0% accuracy on FF++ (HQ), 96.15% on FF++ (LQ), 99.8% on Celeb-DF, 92.1% on DFDC.
- M2TR (2022): AUC of 99.51 (FF++ HQ), 99.92 (FF++ RAW), 95.5 (Celeb-DF), 86.7 (SR-DF).
- Wang et al. (2023): 92.11% accuracy and 97.66% AUC on FF++, but cross-dataset AUC drops to 65.76 (DFDC), 63.27 (Celeb-DF), 62.46 (DF-1.0).

A "SoK: Systematization and Benchmarking of Deepfake Detectors" study (https://arxiv.org/html/2401.04364v4) reviewed 51 detectors published 2019–2023, identified 18 critical factors, and built the first "white-box" deepfake dataset to evaluate 16 state-of-the-art detectors under black-box, gray-box, and white-box conditions.

### 2.2 Diffusion-Model and GAN Image Forensics

Detection of diffusion-generated images has emerged as a distinct sub-field. Ricker et al. (2024; https://www.scitepress.org/Papers/2024/124220/124220.pdf) showed that (a) state-of-the-art GAN detectors fail to reliably detect diffusion-generated images, but (b) re-training them on diffusion-generated images yields near-perfect detection that generalizes back to GANs. They attribute the difficulty to the absence of the grid-like frequency artifacts typical of GANs.

More recent universal detectors include:

- ZED (Zero-shot Entropy-based Detector; https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.15875): Achieves a 3%+ average accuracy improvement over prior SoTA across a wide range of generators without needing AI-generated training data.
- TSG (Time Step Generating; https://arxiv.org/html/2411.11016v2): Uses a pre-trained diffusion network as feature extractor by varying the time step t; reports significant improvements on the GenImage benchmark.
- APN (Artifact Purification Network; https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1016/j.cviu.2024.104078): Achieves 5.6–16.4% higher accuracy on GenImage and 1.7–50.1% on DiffusionForensics for cross-generator detection.
- LoL (Learning on Less; https://arxiv.org/html/2412.00665): With only 1% of training data, achieves a 13.6% average accuracy improvement across 8 diffusion models.
- Community Forensics (https://arxiv.org/html/2411.04125v1): 2.7 million images from 4,803 different generators; shows that detector generalization improves with both quantity and diversity of generators in training data.
- Wavelet-CLIP (https://arxiv.org/html/2409.18301v3): Average AUC of 0.749 for cross-data generalization and 0.893 for unseen deepfake robustness.
- D³ Discrepancy Deepfake Detector (https://arxiv.org/html/2404.04584v1): 5.3% accuracy improvement in out-of-domain testing on UFD/GenImage while maintaining in-domain performance.

---

## 3. Technical Methods for Audio Deepfake Detection

### 3.1 End-to-End Architectures

RawNet2 and AASIST have been the two dominant end-to-end architectures. RawNet2 ingests raw waveforms and applies SincNet filters, while AASIST combines a RawNet2-based encoder with heterogeneous stacking graph attention layers and a "max graph operation" (https://mm.kaist.ac.kr/pubs/pdfs/jung22c.pdf). Improvements since 2022 include:

- ARawNet2 (Li et al., Interspeech 2023; https://www.isca-archive.org/interspeech_2023/li23h_interspeech.pdf): Adds an attention-based channel masking block; achieves EER of 4.61% on ASVspoof 2019 LA, 8.36% on ASVspoof 2021 LA, and 19.03% on ASVspoof 2021 DF—relative EER reductions of 12.00% and 14.97% over the RawNet2 baseline.
- AASIST2 (https://arxiv.org/html/2309.08279): Replaces residual blocks with Res2Net blocks, applies Dynamic Chunk Size (DCS) and Adaptive Large Margin Fine-Tuning (ALMFT) for improved short-utterance evaluation.
- AASIST3 with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (https://www.isca-archive.org/asvspoof_2024/borodin24_asvspoof.pdf): Achieves minDCF of 0.5357 in closed condition and 0.1414 in open condition for ASVspoof 5, with 22.67% EER (closed) and 4.89% EER (open)—more than a two-fold improvement over the baseline.
- CoNSIST (KIPS 2024; https://www.manuscriptlink.com/society/kips/conference/ask2024): Adds Squeeze-and-Excitation, Positional Encoding, and reformulated HS-GAL to AASIST.
- TO-RawNet (https://www.isca-archive.org/interspeech_2023/wang23w_interspeech.pdf): Combines orthogonal regularization on Sinc-conv filters with Temporal Convolutional Networks; reports a 66.09% relative EER reduction on ASVspoof 2019 LA compared with RawNet.
- Whisper+AASIST (https://faculty.cs.gwu.edu/xiaodongqu/papers/HCII_2024_572_Whisper_Qian.pdf): Combines OpenAI Whisper with AASIST; reports competitive performance on the 2021 ASVspoof DF subset and surpasses baselines on in-the-wild audio datasets.
- wav2vec 2.0 + AASIST (https://arxiv.org/html/2402.17127): Examines layer selection and fine-tuning strategies for wav2vec 2.0; achieves state-of-the-art performance on ASVspoof 2019 LA.

### 3.2 ASVspoof 5 Challenge Results (2024)

ASVspoof 5 (Wang et al., 2024; https://arxiv.org/html/2408.08739v1) introduced crowdsourced data with greater acoustic variation, neural codecs, and adversarial attacks. Two tracks were defined: standalone CM (Track 1) and spoofing-robust ASV (Track 2). New metrics include minDCF, actDCF, C_llr (Track 1), and a-DCF (Track 2). Reported results:

- ParallelChain Lab ensemble: minDCF of 0.2660 on Track 1 closed condition (https://www.isca-archive.org/asvspoof_2024/tran24_asvspoof.pdf).
- USTC-KXDIGIT: 0.3948 minDCF and 14.33% EER (Track 1 closed), 0.0750 minDCF and 2.59% EER (Track 1 open) (https://www.isca-archive.org/asvspoof_2024/chen24_asvspoof.pdf).
- SHADOW team FwSE-ResNet34 with codec augmentation: minDCF = 0.44 on Track 1 Eval set (47% improvement over baseline); a-DCF = 0.397 on Track 2 (42% improvement) (https://www.isca-archive.org/asvspoof_2024/villalba24_asvspoof.pdf).

The ASVspoof 2024 workshop summary noted substantial improvements over baselines in open conditions, but a significant gap between progress and evaluation sets, and that adversarial attacks, neural codecs, and non-studio quality data remain challenging.

### 3.3 Interpretable Audio Detection

SLIM (Style-Linguistics Mismatch; https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/7d6930fd71740eae21224a5ffb70cb8c-Paper-Conference.pdf) uses self-supervised pretraining on real samples to learn style-linguistics dependencies; provides interpretable "mismatch" scores. TADA (Targeted Augmented Data; https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.07598) applies adversarial training-time augmentation for RawNet2 and AASIST to improve robustness.

---

## 4. Cross-Dataset Generalization

Cross-dataset generalization remains the central open problem. The 2024 systematic review (https://www.mdpi.com/2673-2688/7/2/68) found that detection systems suffer an average 10–15% performance drop across all methodological classes, with strong evidence that models learn "dataset-specific compression artifacts rather than deepfake characteristics that are generalizable."

The SoK paper (https://arxiv.org/html/2401.04364v4) reports large generalization drops when moving from intra-dataset to cross-dataset evaluations. In "Cross-Dataset Deepfake Detection: Evaluating the Generalization Capabilities of Modern DeepFake Detectors" (CVWW 2024; https://cvww2024.sdrv.si/wp-content/uploads/sites/5/2024/08/Cross-Dataset_Deepfake_Detection_Evaluating_the_Generalization_Capabilities_of_Modern_DeepFake_Detectors.pdf), training on one FaceForensics++ sub-method and testing on another yielded AUCs ranging from 0.5050 to 0.9974, confirming extreme variability across manipulation types.

A Berkeley iSchool paper (https://www.ischool.berkeley.edu/sites/default/files/bb_paper.pdf) showed that fine-tuned CLIP-based detectors achieve strong in-domain generalization but no method achieved meaningful zero-shot generalization, although rehearsal learning showed consistent patterns in how training on one generative model impacts performance on others.

---

## 5. Foundation Model Integration (CLIP, Vision-Language Models)

Foundation models, particularly CLIP, have become a major research direction for generalizable detection since 2023.

- CLIPping the Deception (Khan & Dang-Nguyen, ICMR 2024; https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.12927): Uses prompt tuning on CLIP with only 200k images; outperforms prior SOTA by 5.01% mAP and 6.61% accuracy while using less than one-third of the training data; evaluated on 21 distinct datasets including GAN, diffusion, and commercial tools.
- C2P-CLIP (https://arxiv.org/html/2408.09647v2): Injects category common prompts; achieves 12.41% accuracy improvement over vanilla CLIP, no extra inference parameters.
- Forensics Adapter (https://arxiv.org/html/2411.19715v3): Only 5.7M trainable parameters; approximately 7% average improvement across five datasets; Forensics Adapter++ adds textual modality for +1.3%.
- CLIPMoLE (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2404.04883): Fine-tunes only 0.08% of parameters using mixture-of-LoRAs experts; outperforms baseline by +3.64% mAP and +12.72% avg accuracy across unseen diffusion and autoregressive models.
- "Standing on the Shoulders of Giants" (https://arxiv.org/html/2409.02664v4): Uses model reprogramming with learnable visual perturbations and face-embedding-based adaptive text prompts; achieves over 88% AUC cross-dataset (FF++ → WildDeepfake).
- PromptFake (Springer 2025; https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-981-95-5761-5_38): Combines learnable textual prompts with layer-wise feature decoupling on CLIP.
- Wavelet-CLIP (https://arxiv.org/html/2409.18301v3): Combines wavelet transforms with CLIP ViT-L/14 features; average AUC 0.749 (cross-data) and 0.893 (unseen deepfakes).
- DeCLIP (https://arxiv.org/html/2409.08849): First attempt to use CLIP features for deepfake localization (not just detection), including challenging latent-diffusion cases.
- "Towards More General Video-based Deepfake Detection" (https://arxiv.org/html/2404.05583v2): Uses CLIP's image encoder with side-network decoder and Facial Component Guidance; 0.9% AUROC average improvement cross-dataset, with 4.4% lead on the challenging DFDC dataset.

The community-forensics / GenImage / CLIP-MoLE line of work consistently shows that (a) training-data diversity drives generalization more than architecture, and (b) parameter-efficient fine-tuning of CLIP largely preserves the zero-shot transfer properties of the foundation model.

---

## 6. Multimodal Audio-Visual Detection

Recognizing that a single modality is increasingly insufficient, 2023–2024 research has emphasized audio-visual fusion:

- AVA-CL (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3625100): Joint audio-visual attention with contrastive learning; uses MARLIN as a face representation model; claims superior robustness and generalization over SOTA.
- AVFF (Oorloff et al., CVPR 2024; https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2024/papers/Oorloff_AVFF_Audio-Visual_Feature_Fusion_for_Video_Deepfake_Detection_CVPR_2024_paper.pdf): Two-stage cross-modal learning via self-supervision on real videos using contrastive learning, autoencoding, and complementary masking; reports 98.6% accuracy and 99.1% AUC on FakeAVCeleb (14.9% and 9.9% gains over prior SOTA).
- ART-AVDF (https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1016/j.cviu.2024.104133): Articulatory representation learning; tested on DFDC, FakeAVCeleb, and DefakeAVMiT.
- AV-LGNN (ACM MM 2024; https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/3664647.3688985): Audio-Visual Local-Global Interaction Module; submitted to the Video-Level Deepfake Detection challenge at ACM Multimedia 2024.
- MFMS (ACM MM 2024; https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3664647.3688984): Top performance in the AV-Deepfake1M competition; modality-fused and modality-specific feature learning.
- SpeechForensics (NeurIPS 2024; https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/9c7900fac04a701cbed83256b76dbaa3-Paper-Conference.pdf): Self-supervised masked-prediction on real videos to learn audio-visual speech representations, then transferred directly to forgery detection; outperforms SOTA on cross-dataset generalization and robustness without using any fake video in training.
- "Zero-Shot Fake Video Detection by Audio-Visual Consistency" (Interspeech 2024; https://www.isca-archive.org/interspeech_2024/li24ta_interspeech.pdf): Uses pre-trained ASR and VSR models; computes edit distance between recognized audio and video content sequences; achieves strong generalization across deepfake techniques.
- MSOC (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.14176): Multi-Stream Fusion with One-Class Learning; extends one-class learning to audio-visual setting; benchmarks on four FakeAVCeleb splits (RAFV, FAFV, FARV, Unsynced).
- The "Evolving from Single-modal to Multi-modal Facial Deepfake Detection" survey (https://arxiv.org/html/2406.06965v1) documents the field's transition through June 2024.

---

## 7. Privacy-Preserving Detection Techniques

Since 2022, several lines of work have tackled the privacy implications of centralized detection training:

- FedForgery (https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2210.09563): Variational autoencoder for residual feature maps combined with general federated learning for face-forgery detection across distributed clients.
- Dynamic-Aware Federated Learning for Face Forgery Video Detection (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3501814): First FL framework for face forgery with an Inconsistency-Capture module capturing global and local inter-frame inconsistencies.
- Blockchain-based FL for deepfake detection (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12559-024-10255-7): Combines SegCaps + CNN feature extraction with capsule-network training, blockchain-based FL aggregation; reports 6.6% accuracy and 5.1% AUC improvements over six baselines.
- FLADD (Federated Learning for Audio Deepfake Detection; https://eurekamag.com/research/110/713/110713846.php): Dual-branch Res2Net + Rawformer with Multi-Factor Adaptive Weighting and dual-prototype strategy; achieves best Equal Error Rates of 0.285% on ASVspoof 2019 LA and 2.045% on ASVspoof 2021 LA evaluation sets.
- FL-TENB4 (https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/d97c/1fd280a818f9a30435c07717effc18a1cc08.pdf): Tiny EfficientNetB4-Lite + FL for CCTV environments; designed for edge deployment with minimal latency.
- FedMaxAdapt (https://researchonline.gcu.ac.uk/ws/portalfiles/portal/113968862/113434712.pdf): Adaptive sparsity via gradient-guided per-layer pruning; reduces bandwidth by 43.1% (video) and 40.3% (audio) at 50% sparsity; 90.1% video accuracy and 91.0% audio accuracy.
- "Robust Detection of Deepfake Images in Blockchain Systems Using Differential Privacy and Secure Multi-Party Computation" (https://exa.ai/library/publication/0l8tfgks3zx): Achieves 98.4% accuracy on the DeepFake Detection Challenge dataset; PSNR of 46.2 dB for privacy-preserving image quality.
- Interpretable-Aware Privacy Preserving Framework (https://www.researchsquare.com/article/rs-10197752/latest.pdf): Federated ResNet-18 + FedProx + Explainable AI on FaceForensics++.
- Cognitive-Inspired Multimodal Framework (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12559-026-10640-4): Reports 98.32% accuracy on FoR (audio), 99.43% on SDFVD (video), and 99.87% on TweepFake (text).
- FMM-MMF (https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s10791-026-10073-5.pdf): Federated micro-expression mining and multi-modal metadata fusion for V-KYC fraud detection; 96.74% accuracy and 0.987 F1 under non-IID conditions.

---

## 8. Benchmark vs. Real-World Deployment Performance

The single most important empirical result of 2024–2025 is the magnitude of the benchmark-to-deployment gap.

**Deepfake-Eval-2024** (Chandra et al., CVPRW 2025/2026; https://arxiv.org/html/2503.02857v4, https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2026W/APAI/papers/Chandra_Deepfake-Eval-2024_A_Multi-Modal_In-the-Wild_Benchmark_of_Deepfakes_Circulated_in_2024_CVPRW_2026_paper.pdf) collected 45 hours of video, 56.5 hours of audio, and 1,975 images from 88 different websites in 52 languages. Compared to original benchmark AUCs near 1.0:

| Modality | Model | Original AUC | Deepfake-Eval-2024 AUC | Drop |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Video | GenConViT | 0.96 | 0.63 | ~34% |
| Video | FTCN | 0.87 | 0.50 | ~37% |
| Video | Styleflow | 0.95 | 0.51 | ~44% |
| Audio | AASIST | 1.00 | 0.43 | ~57% |
| Audio | RawNet2 | 0.99 | 0.53 | ~46% |
| Audio | P3 | 1.00 | 0.58 | ~42% |
| Image | UFD | 0.94 | 0.56 | ~38% |
| Image | DistilDIRE | 0.99 | 0.52 | ~47% |
| Image | NPR | 0.98 | 0.53 | ~45% |

The authors report aggregate AUC drops of approximately 50% for video, 48% for audio, and 45% for image models. Fine-tuning on Deepfake-Eval-2024 improves accuracy to 61–69%, and the best commercial detector reaches 82% accuracy—still below expert forensic analysts. A subsequent paper (https://arxiv.org/html/2509.04150v1) showed that the simple Ojha-style CLIP-based baseline, with better-tuned hyperparameters, achieves 81% accuracy on Deepfake-Eval-2024, gaining 18 percentage points over the original report and matching commercial systems.

**Other independent evidence**:
- "Evaluating Deepfake Detectors in the Wild" (SumSubstance; https://arxiv.org/html/2507.21905): Fewer than half of tested detectors achieved AUC > 60%, with the lowest at 50%; JPEG compression and image enhancement cause additional large drops.
- "VendorBench-100" (https://arxiv.org/html/2607.06254v2): Evaluates 36 models under edge-case conditions; finds commercial APIs strongest, followed by vision-LLMs, with open-source detectors competitive with the best LLMs; strong correlation (Pearson r ≈ 0.86) between MCC and ROC-AUC.
- "How well are open sourced AI-generated image detection models out-of-the-box" (https://arxiv.org/html/2602.07814): A 37-percentage-point gap separates the best detector (75.0% mean accuracy) from the worst (37.5%); modern commercial generators (Flux Dev, Firefly v4, Midjourney v7) defeat most detectors, achieving only 18–30% average accuracy.
- "Analyzing Commercial Deepfake Detectors on Real-World Cases" (https://dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3803629.3803675): Commercial detectors achieve stronger out-of-domain generalization than academic baselines but are influenced by aggregation strategies, mosaic artifacts, and reliance on face detection.
- "Towards Real-World Deepfake Detection: RedFace" (https://arxiv.org/html/2510.08067v1): 60,000 forged images from 9 commercial online platforms; existing detectors fail to generalize.
- "The Deployment Gap in AI Media Detection" (https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2026W/AIMS/papers/Budhkar_The_Deployment_Gap_in_AI_Media_Detection_Platform-Aware_and_Visually_CVPRW_2026_paper.pdf): Detectors achieving AUC ≈ 0.99 in clean settings suffer substantial degradation under platform-aware attacks, with pronounced calibration collapse.

In short, the field exhibits a roughly two-orders-of-magnitude reality gap: 90–99% accuracy on academic benchmarks translates to 40–60% accuracy on real-world content, with even the best commercial systems hovering around 80%.

---

## 9. Proactive Detection, Watermarking, and Provenance

Complementing passive detection, 2023–2024 work explored proactive defenses:

- AdvMark (IJCAI 2024; https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2024/0673.pdf): Fine-tunes robust watermarks into adversarial watermarks to enhance downstream deepfake detector accuracy.
- LampMark (https://arxiv.org/html/2411.17209v1): Training-free landmark perceptual watermarks using facial landmarks; superior cross-dataset and cross-manipulation performance.
- ProMark (CVPR 2024; https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2024/papers/Asnani_ProMark_Proactive_Diffusion_Watermarking_for_Causal_Attribution_CVPR_2024_paper.pdf): Embeds up to 2^16 unique watermarks into training data for causal attribution.
- ZoDiac (NeurIPS 2024; https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/43d33182360378d5c8e69dd706c24f2f-Paper-Conference.pdf): Uses a pre-trained Stable Diffusion latent space for watermarking; >98% watermark detection rate and <6.4% false-positive rate under attacks.
- RAW (NeurIPS 2024; https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/ee62ab636066cf45a27246acca9545b7-Paper-Conference.pdf): Learnable watermarks with provable false-positive guarantees via conformal prediction.
- GAN-based Visible Watermarking (https://soar.wichita.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/32c84b70-c0d9-493d-a2cd-188bcc5a8f92/content): Embeds unique watermarks into generated fake images themselves.
- C2PA Content Provenance (https://spec.c2pa.org/specifications/specifications/1.3/specs/C2PA_Specification.html): Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity standard using cryptographically signed manifests; supported by major media and tech companies.

---

## 10. Ethical Concerns

Researchers have consistently identified the following ethical issues:

1. **Non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII / deepfake pornography)**: A 10-country survey of 16,000+ respondents found 2.2% personal victimization and 1.8% perpetration rates, even in jurisdictions with specific legislation (https://dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3613904.3642382). The 2024 UK Online Safety Act analysis (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0267364924000906) argues existing platform-based remedies are insufficient.

2. **Election and political misinformation**: Recorded Future identified 82 deepfakes impersonating public figures between July 2023 and July 2024 across 38 countries; 26.8% promoted financially motivated scams, 25.6% fabricated misleading statements, 15.8% were electioneering, 10.9% character assassination, 10.9% non-consensual pornography (https://assets.recordedfuture.com/insikt-report-pdfs/2024/ta-2024-0924.pdf). A WIRED-based analysis of 78 election deepfakes (Knight First Amendment Institute; https://knightcolumbia.org/blog/we-looked-at-78-election-deepfakes-political-misinformation-is-not-an-ai-problem) found that non-AI "cheap fakes" were used seven times more often than AI-generated content, but AI deepfakes still pose disproportionate risks via the "liar's dividend."

3. **The liar's dividend**: Research at Purdue's GRAIL lab (https://www.brookings.edu/articles/watch-out-for-false-claims-of-deepfakes-and-actual-deepfakes-this-election-year/) documents how politicians may falsely dismiss real evidence as AI-generated.

4. **Categorization of harms**: Typology work (https://exa.ai/library/publication/h1jywj8cntt) analyzing 50 incidents found relational harm (64%), systemic, financial, and emotional harm common beyond NCII.

5. **Bias in detectors and training data**: The German survey on AI inequalities (https://a-mcc.eu/backend/gpt/pdfs/deepfakes-in-the-context-of-ai-inequalities-analysing-disparities-in-knowledge-and-attitudes.pdf) found that gender, age, and educational attainment predict deepfake knowledge, raising concerns about equitable protection.

6. **Detection ethics**: Papers including the SOUPS 2024 study (https://www.usenix.org/conference/soups2024/presentation/brigham) document public attitudes opposing creation and especially sharing of non-consensual synthetic intimate imagery, with significant variation by creator relationship and gender.

7. **Privacy in detection systems**: Federated-learning work explicitly addresses the tension between centralized detection (better accuracy) and decentralized training (preserving user data locality under GDPR and similar regimes).

---

## 11. Regulatory Frameworks

### 11.1 European Union — AI Act

Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (https://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=OJ%3AL_202401689) was adopted on 13 June 2024. Key deepfake-relevant provisions:

- **Article 50(4)** — Deployers of AI systems that generate or manipulate image, audio, or video content constituting a "deep fake" must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated. Exceptions: content used for authorized law-enforcement purposes; or content forming part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional, or analogous work, where disclosure is limited to indicating the existence of synthetic content in a manner that does not hamper the work.
- **Article 50(2)** — Providers of AI systems generating synthetic audio, image, video, or text must ensure outputs are marked in a machine-readable format as artificially generated or manipulated.
- **Article 50(5)** — Information must be provided "in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of the first interaction or exposure."
- **Recital 134** (https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/recital-134): Disclosure obligation is "limited to disclosure of the existence of such generated or manipulated content in an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work."

**Effective dates**: Article 50 applies from 2 August 2026 (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/guidelines-ai-transparency-obligations). The Commission has published Guidelines on the implementation of Article 50 transparency obligations and a voluntary Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content (Sections 1 and 2 respectively address provider marking/detection and deployer labeling of deepfakes and AI text). National market surveillance authorities, the AI Office, and the European Data Protection Supervisor (for EU institutions) enforce the rules.

### 11.2 United States

**Federal TAKE IT DOWN Act** (Pub. L. 119-12; https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-bill/146, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/COMPS-18158/pdf/COMPS-18158.pdf, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TAKE_IT_DOWN_Act). Sponsored by Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX), passed Senate by unanimous consent on 13 February 2025 and the House 409-2 on 28 April 2025; signed by President Trump on 19 May 2025. Key provisions:

- **Section 2**: Amends Section 223 of the Communications Act of 1934 (47 U.S.C. 223) to add subsection (h) — criminal prohibition on intentional disclosure of non-consensual intimate visual depictions, including "digital forgeries" defined as any intimate visual depiction "created through the use of software, machine learning, artificial intelligence, or any other computer-generated or technological means."
- **Penalties**: Up to 2 years' imprisonment for offenses involving adults (3 years when the depiction involves a minor), in addition to fines and mandatory restitution. Threats to publish are similarly prohibited.
- **Section 3**: Requires "covered platforms" to establish a notice-and-removal process within one year (i.e., by 19 May 2026) and to remove flagged content within 48 hours of a valid notice. Failure to comply constitutes an unfair or deceptive act under FTC jurisdiction.

**State laws**: According to the comprehensive review at https://exa.ai/library/publication/dtbv24df4gm and the Jones Walker analysis (https://www.joneswalker.com/en/insights/blogs/ai-law-blog/deepfakes-as-a-service-meets-state-laws-governing-synthetic-media-in-fragmente.html), 46 states have enacted deepfake legislation since 2022, with 169 laws total and 146 bills introduced in 2025 alone. Major examples:

- **Texas Election Code § 255.004** (2019): Criminalizes creation of deepfake videos within 30 days of an election (some provisions challenged constitutionally).
- **Minnesota Statutes § 609.771**: Extends coverage to 90 days before a political convention; escalating felony penalties for repeat offenses.
- **Virginia Code § 18.2-386.2** (2019): First state criminal penalties for distribution of intimate imagery.
- **Tennessee ELVIS Act**: First state law explicitly protecting voice as a right of publicity in the AI context.

**Earlier federal action**: The 2022 Violence Against Women Act reauthorization established a federal civil right of action for victims of non-consensual pornography, though its applicability to AI-generated imagery was unsettled. The FCC has also banned AI-generated voices in robocalls (https://www.brookings.edu/articles/watch-out-for-false-claims-of-deepfakes-and-actual-deepfakes-this-election-year/).

### 11.3 China

**Provisions on the Administration of Deep Synthesis of Internet-based Information Services** (Order No. 12; https://www.cac.gov.cn/2022-12/11/c_1672221949318230.htm, https://www.loc.gov/item/global-legal-monitor/2023-04-25/china-provisions-on-deep-synthesis-technology-enter-into-effect/, https://www.gov.cn/gongbao/content/2023/content_5741257.htm). Adopted by the Cyberspace Administration of China together with the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and the Ministry of Public Security on 25 November 2022; effective 10 January 2023. Key provisions:

- Article 6: Prohibits use of deep-synthesis services to produce or disseminate information prohibited by law or to fabricate false news.
- Article 7: Service providers must establish internal review, ethics, and security mechanisms.
- Article 9: Mandatory real-identity authentication of users (via mobile number, ID, or national network-identity authentication).
- Article 10: Content moderation via technical or manual review; establishment of illegal-content feature databases.
- Article 11: Mandatory rumor-refutation mechanism; reports to authorities on detection of fake news.
- Articles 14–15: Training-data management; safety assessments for tools generating biometric features (face, voice) or special non-biometric content.
- **Articles 16–17**: Mandatory visible marking for content produced by services that "may lead to public confusion or misidentification" (including smart dialogue, voice generation, face generation/replacement/manipulation, and immersive virtual scenes). Article 18 makes deletion, alteration, or concealment of these marks illegal.
- Articles 19–20: Mandatory algorithm filing for services with opinion-forming or social-mobilization capabilities; security assessments before launching new products.

**Companion regulation**: Interim Measures for the Management of Generative AI Services (Order No. 15; effective 15 August 2023; https://www.gov.cn/gongbao/2023/issue_10666/202308/content_6900864.html) applies to providers of generative AI services and explicitly cross-references the Deep Synthesis Provisions for content marking (Article 12).

### 11.4 United Kingdom and Other Jurisdictions

- **UK Online Safety Act 2023**: Contains offences related to sharing intimate images without consent, but research (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0267364924000906) argues its content-moderation approach is insufficient for non-consensual intimate deepfakes.
- **South Korea**: Amendments to the Information and Communications Network Act and the Telecommunications Business Act in 2024–2025 require explicit labeling of AI-generated content.
- **Japan**: Voluntary guidelines from the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications and discussions toward binding rules.
- **International**: The Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI (opened for signature in September 2024; not yet in force) addresses transparency and risk management obligations that intersect with deepfake disclosure.

---

## 12. Quantitative Summary

Aggregating the benchmark results cited above:

| Task | Best in-dataset (academic) | Best real-world (in-the-wild) | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| Image deepfake detection | AUC ~0.95–0.99 (UFD, NPR on academic datasets) | AUC ~0.52–0.56 on Deepfake-Eval-2024; best commercial ~0.82 accuracy | ~40–50% AUC |
| Audio deepfake detection | EER ~0.5–2% (AASIST, RawNet2 on ASVspoof 2019 LA) | AUC 0.43–0.58 on Deepfake-Eval-2024; ASVspoof 5 best minDCF 0.266 (closed) | ~50% AUC drop |
| Video deepfake detection | AUC 0.95–0.99 on FF++ (Xception, ViT variants) | AUC 0.50–0.63 on Deepfake-Eval-2024; best commercial ~82% accuracy | ~30–50% AUC drop |

Cross-dataset generalization gaps within academic benchmarks: ~11–15% AUC decline for transformer-based and CNN-based detectors respectively; 25–40% for older CNN architectures.

State-of-the-art on ASVspoof 5 (closed condition): best minDCF 0.2660 (ParallelChain Lab); best EER 2.20–2.59% (multiple submissions). On open condition with self-supervised features (USTC-KXDIGIT): minDCF 0.0750, EER 2.59%.

---

## 13. Conclusion and Outlook

Since 2022, deepfake detection research has matured significantly in architectural sophistication—transformer-based, CLIP-adapted, audio-visual, articulatory, and foundation-model approaches have collectively raised in-domain performance to saturation (>95% AUC on standard benchmarks). However, three persistent realities define the current state of the field:

1. **The deployment gap**: Models near-perfect on academic datasets perform near chance on real-world social-media content (Deepfake-Eval-2024: 45–50% AUC drops across modalities). Closing this gap requires broader and more current training corpora (community forensics style), modality-aware evaluation, and platform-aware adversarial robustness testing.

2. **The architectural plateau**: Empirical evidence suggests that within an architectural class, training-data diversity drives generalization more than model size or attention mechanism. Foundation-model adaptation (CLIP with PEFT) and federated / privacy-preserving training have emerged as the most promising directions for moving beyond the plateau.

3. **The regulatory momentum**: The EU AI Act, US TAKE IT DOWN Act, and China's Deep Synthesis Provisions together establish a global baseline of disclosure-and-labeling obligations, with enforcement dates beginning in mid-2025 (US) and 2026 (EU). These rules position detection and watermarking as compliance infrastructure rather than purely research problems.

Unresolved challenges include: cross-generator generalization to unseen diffusion architectures, robustness to compression and platform transformations, multimodal consistency checking at video level, federated and on-device deployment under privacy constraints, harmonized provenance standards (C2PA, watermarking), and detection in the presence of deliberate adversarial countermeasures. Researchers are increasingly framing deepfake detection not as a forensic arms race but as a socio-technical system in which detection, provenance, regulation, and media literacy operate together.

# Adaptive Input Systems for Musicians with Hand Tremor in DAW Environments: A Critical Synthesis of Available Evidence

## 1. Executive summary and important caveats about the original premises

The original brief asks for a comparison among three named systems — "Ableton Live's MIDI velocity smoothing," "Logic Pro's Smart Controls with tremor compensation," and "SteadyMouse" — and demands HCI evidence on tremor-vs-vibrato discrimination, false-positive rates for gesture rejection, and motor-skill retention. After exhaustive searching of primary documentation and peer-reviewed sources, three of those premises cannot be verified and must be flagged before any synthesis:

- **Logic Pro's Smart Controls do not contain a documented "tremor compensation" feature.** Apple's own user guide describes Smart Controls only as "on-screen controls" that adapt plug-in and channel-strip parameters for a selected track (https://support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/smart-controls-overview-lgcp7e59f24b/mac). The Logic Pro accessibility conformance (VPAT) report confirms accessibility is delegated to macOS-level features — VoiceOver, Switch Control, keyboard navigation, Zoom — and never describes any "tremor compensation" mode in Smart Controls (https://support.apple.com/content/dam/edam/applecare/images/en_US/otherassets/accessibility/vpat_logic_pro_2024.pdf).
- **Ableton Live has general-purpose MIDI velocity utilities, not a productized "tremor compensation" feature.** Live 12's accessibility additions — screen-reader support, keyboard navigation, high-contrast theme — target vision-impaired and keyboard-only users (https://www.ableton.com/en/live-manual/12/accessibility-options-in-live/).
- **There is no peer-reviewed HCI paper that benchmarks composition completion time or user satisfaction specifically against tremor-filter sensitivity thresholds in DAW contexts.** The studies that exist are either non-musical (gesture-rejection HCI), adjacent to music (vocal vibrato vs. tremor detection), or single-case reports of individual musicians.

What does exist in the literature is sufficient to give a well-grounded picture of how current systems behave, where they fail, and what designing better ones requires. The remainder of this report is grounded exclusively in those documented sources.

---

## 2. Documented platform features

### 2.1 Ableton Live — MIDI effects usable for tremor, by user workaround

Live's **Velocity** MIDI effect (Live 12 reference, §30.8) does *not* advertise a tremor-related mode, but its behavior is exactly what a tremor user needs: it can **Gate** incoming MIDI notes whose velocity falls outside a configured range, discarding the rest. Specifically, the documentation states: "In Gate mode, incoming velocities outside the range are removed altogether" (https://www.ableton.com/en/live-manual/12/live-midi-effect-reference/). The same device exposes a Curve grid mapping, with **Clip**, **Fixed**, and **Random** modes — Random injects jitter around the curve within a configurable band, while Clip silently drops anything outside the band. A 2009 user thread on the Ableton forum explicitly identifies the Gate workaround for this problem: "use gate mode in the Velocity device, and set the 'lowest' slider to 25, 30, etc. basically adjust it til it no longer picks up the quiet notes. only the velocities over 25, 35 etc will make it through" (https://forum.ableton.com/viewtopic.php?t=120139). The complementary **Note Length** and **Pitch** MIDI effects can additionally shape timing and pitch-bleed artifacts. None of these filters carry latency budgets or confidence scores; they are deterministic MIDI math.

Live's *accessibility* surface (added in 12) is unrelated to tremor: it's screen-reader compatibility, Tab-navigation, Speak Help Text, and high-contrast theme (https://www.ableton.com/en/live-manual/12/accessibility-options-in-live/).

### 2.2 Logic Pro — no tremor compensation in Smart Controls

The "Smart Controls" mechanism in Logic Pro is a **controller mapping layer**, not an input filter. From Apple's reference manual: "Each Smart Control has a set of screen controls. Adjusting a single screen control can change one or more parameters for the track's channel strip, instrument, and effect plug-ins" (https://support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/smart-controls-overview-lgcp7e59f24b/mac). It supports Expert-view parameter mapping, hardware controller assignment, and articulation switching — none of which is "tremor compensation."

The Logic Pro accessibility VPAT (https://support.apple.com/content/dam/edam/applecare/images/en_US/otherassets/accessibility/vpat_logic_pro_2024.pdf) lists the platform's actual accommodations:

| User need | Documented support |
|---|---|
| Blind / low vision | VoiceOver, scalable cursor, Zoom, braille displays |
| Limited reach / simultaneous actions | Switch Control |
| Limited manual dexterity | macOS Sticky Keys, Slow Keys, Mouse Keys |

The only Logic-side remediation that overlaps with tremor is **macOS Mouse Keys** (numeric-keypad cursor emulation), which removes the need for fine mouse control entirely. This is a host-OS feature, not a Logic feature. Practitioners seeking tremor accommodation in Logic overwhelmingly rely on (a) external hardware with their own anti-tremor firmware (e.g. specialized keyboards or alternative controllers), (b) host-level assistive tools like SteadyMouse on Windows or built-in macOS pointer smoothing, and (c) tracks of pre-quantized MIDI rather than live performance capture.

### 2.3 SteadyMouse — direct, but cursor-level, not MIDI-level

SteadyMouse 2 (manual dated January 2026; https://www.steadymouse.com/manual/) is the most extensively documented tremor filter for desktop interaction. It works at the OS cursor layer, so it operates transparently on *every* application — including any DAW — but it does not understand MIDI semantics.

Documented features relevant to creative work:

- **Seven filter sets**, each trading snappiness for tremor removal: *Allegro* (default medium), *Feather* (snappiest, formerly called "Gaming"), *Adagio* (heavy, laggy but powerful), *Classic* (v1 heritage), *Artistry* (smooth curves for drawing), *Laggy* (extreme tremor), *Steadicam* (new in 2.8.2.0, for camera-style stabilization).
- A **filter strength slider**, with the explicit tuning procedure the vendor documents: "Start with mouse speed below ten percent and filter strength around 95%… then decrease strength until tremor just begins to reappear" (https://www.steadymouse.com/manual/).
- **Click-duration gating** that drops mouse clicks shorter than a configurable threshold — i.e., distinguishing accidental taps from intentional ones by hold time.
- An **Icon Targeting** snap-to-target mode that lets a user double-tap a modifier key to commit to the nearest clickable element.
- **Auto-disable of Windows "Enhanced Pointer Precision"** because it "actually degrades precision" — relevant because that setting also affects MIDI controller fader mapping in DAWs.
- A **Num-Lock (or Scroll-Lock) global on/off toggle** so a user can switch back to raw cursor input when doing fine calibrated work (e.g., editing automation curves).

SteadyMouse's limits are equally clear. It is **Windows-only**; a Mac port is acknowledged as "extremely difficult" and not yet released (https://www.steadymouse.com/manual/). It cannot distinguish intentional vibrato-like mid-pitch MIDI modulation from involuntary 4–7 Hz oscillation because, at the cursor layer, it has no notion of musical intent. That distinction has to happen further up the stack — in the DAW or in a custom MIDI effect.

---

## 3. HCI research on pathological tremor vs. musical vibrato

### 3.1 Frequency-band overlap is the central problem

The original question's claim that "pathological tremor (4–12 Hz)" can be cleanly separated from "musical expression techniques" is **not supported by the acoustic / motor-control literature**. Pathological tremor and voluntary vibrato overlap heavily in both rate and extent:

| Phenomenon | Reported frequency | Reported extent / character |
|---|---|---|
| Western lyric vocal vibrato | 5–8 Hz, sinusoidal | < ±1.0 semitone (≈ ±6%), low variability (https://pubs.aip.org/asa/jasa/article/130/1/EL1/907816/Vibrato-and-tremor-extent-spectrum-Algorithm-and) |
| Pathological vocal tremor | 4–7 Hz typical, can extend to 3–15 Hz | Greater cycle-to-cycle variability than vibrato; often non-sinusoidal |
| Violin vibrato (voluntary) | ~5–7 Hz dominant, individual-specific | "Almost isometric" flexor-extensor alternation; persistent rhythmic EMG groups (https://exa.ai/library/publication/ddgkqcy2fr5) |
| Primary bowing tremor (pathological, in violinists) | 4.7–6.7 Hz | Wrist flexion-extension; onset ~43 years; treatment overlaps with PWT (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4053556/) |
| Secondary task-specific bowing tremor post-temporal-lobectomy | ~7 Hz | Right-arm-only; coherent with wrist EMG (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4117185/) |
| Pathological tremor band (general) | typically 3–15 Hz | Used as the spectral envelope for tremor suppression filters (http://www.neuralrehabilitation.org/projects/tremor/Documents/deliverables/TREMOR%20D4.1%20update.pdf) |

The 4–12 Hz frame in the question is therefore describing the spectral zone where conflict is maximum, not a clean separator. The literature consistently reports that the *discriminating features are not rate but regularity, shape, and context*: vibrato is sinusoidal and periodic; tremor is more variable and often superimposed on intentional motion (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5392085/; https://exa.ai/library/publication/3fjs73lrd3d).

### 3.2 What an algorithm can — and cannot — infer

A representative tremor vs. vibrato separation framework appears in Boeck, Widmer et al. (ISMIR 2013), "Local Group Delay based Vibrato and Tremolo Suppression for Onset Detection." Their weighting of spectral-flux onset detection by local group delay reduces false onsets caused by vibrato/tremolo energy peaks by **up to 50%** across three corpora: 25,927 mixed onsets, 7,677 violin onsets, and 1,448 opera-singer onsets (https://www.cp.jku.at/research/papers/Boeck_Widmer_Ismir_2013.pdf). Note that this is the *opposite* direction from what a tremor user needs — they want vibrato-style modulation to *pass through*, but the algorithm is built to treat both as spurious onsets. Reusing this for tremor accommodation would require inverting the cost function.

For EMG-level discrimination (closer to what a MIDI exoskeleton might exploit), the Missouri group showed that the **frequency of EMG modulation in ET shifts when voluntary motion is initiated** vs. when the patient is merely holding posture — a "tremor frequency based filter" using an STFT-derived switch achieved partial voluntary-motion preservation that pure low-pass filters damaged (http://vigir.ee.missouri.edu/~gdesouza/Research/Conference_CDs/BioRob_2012/files/0452.pdf). The same group's "optimal digital filtering for tremor suppression" introduced an "equalizer" framework for joystick teleoperation, validated both on artificially-induced vibration and a Parkinson's subject, with the source code archived (https://nemours.elsevierpure.com/en/publications/optimal-digital-filtering-for-tremor-suppression/).

This means there is a *path* to MIDI-level tremor correction — frequency-shift detection at gesture onset — but no peer-reviewed paper has demonstrated it inside a DAW MIDI pipeline. The cognitive load of training such a system per-user, per-session, would be non-trivial.

### 3.3 Gesture rejection HCI: the Voight-Kampff Machine as the closest analogue

The cleanest piece of HCI work on thresholding tremor-like vs. intentional motion is Taranta et al.'s **Voight-Kampff Machine (VKM)**, CHI 2022 (https://cs.ucf.edu/~jjl/pubs/Taranta2022.pdf). VKM is not a tremor filter; it is a *rejection-threshold selector* for custom-gesture recognizers that must decide which continuous-stream inputs to accept as gestures vs. treat as non-gesture noise. The relevance to tremor compensation is direct: any system that filters "the wobble" must decide where the wobble ends and the gesture begins.

Key quantitative findings:

- VKM is the **only threshold-selection technique that consistently achieves high accuracy across four input device types** (pen, mouse, 3D-depth, IMU) on the high-activity gesture datasets tested.
- Quoting Taranta et al.: "loose boundaries can lead to high false positive rates and degrade user experience"; "eliminating false positives is more important than eliminating false negatives" (citing Katsuragawa et al., reference [21] in their paper). A false positive in this domain is *the same failure mode* as a tremor spike passing through to a note — the system misfires on involuntary input.
- VKM's technical contribution is a synthetic-data technique ("Mincer") that produces **negative samples near the gesture boundary**, yielding tighter rejection thresholds than prior splicing techniques (which VKM's authors show are appropriate only for *low-activity* data).
- Empirical tuning parameters reported: training-set size shrinks the threshold (more positive examples → tighter cut); gesture-production variability widens it (gaming/performance contexts are more variable than desktop data-collection contexts, sometimes substantially so — Taranta et al. cite a finding that the same gesture set can have different variability across applications).

The VKM paper is, in effect, an existence proof that **selective tremor rejection is tractable** — but it is bench-tested on drawn gestures, not expressive MIDI parameters. Mapping this to vibrato preservation would require representing both the tremor and the vibrato in the same feature space and tuning VKM to prefer the more periodic of the two.

---

## 4. Documented case studies of musicians with movement disorders in / adjacent to DAWs

### 4.1 Samuel Smith — Parkinson's, AI-mediated workflow (2026)

The most thoroughly documented recent case is London-based singer-songwriter Samuel Smith, diagnosed with Parkinson's in 2020, who released *The Art of Letting Go* in 2026 (https://fortune.com/2026/05/30/parkinsons-ai-music-humming-demos/; https://www.boston.../ai-helped-musician-with-parkinsons-finish-new-album-when-he-could-no-longer-play-guitar/). Smith hums melodies into a phone, uploads them to **Suno** and **Udio**, and edits the AI-generated demos into the final album's instrumental plan. He reports needing **"50, 100, 150 attempts"** per demo before producing something usable (https://aitoolsobserver.com/hub/ai-for-musicians-with-disabilities-inside-samuel-smiths-workflow-with-suno-and-udio/). Critically, the AI demos were not used as the final masters — they were translation layers between his humming and session musicians. This sidesteps the tremor-vs-intent problem entirely by removing the tremor-bearing input modality.

### 4.2 Kira — Essential Tremor, DBS

A touring musician profiled by PMD Alliance in December 2025 (https://www.pmdalliance.org/2025/12/03/touring-musician-kiras-essential-tremor-journey/) reports that prior to deep-brain stimulation she "couldn't play her guitar, and times when she couldn't even get on stage," and that she historically self-medicated with alcohol because prescriptions failed. After a 30 October 2024 DBS procedure, "Immediately, I saw improvement in my right hand. I cried on the operating table as I watched a hand that I felt so disconnected with… show a steadiness." This is a hardware/neurosurgical remediation case, not a DAW-software one — but it documents the magnitude of the symptom set software systems are working against.

### 4.3 Valerie Bryan — Essential Tremor, MRgFUS candidate

A Scottish trad musician with ET published in TRACS (https://tracscotland.org/blog/essential-tremor-a-musicians-perspective-by-valerie-bryan/) documents progressive loss of capability: "I can no longer play the flute or whistle, as I can't really get them to my mouth, let alone hold them there, or play them. (I can still play the piano a bit, and sing, though – I'm lucky!)." She was awaiting Magnetic Resonance-guided Focused Ultrasound treatment. The blog explicitly enumerates DAW-relevant tremor impairments: "playing musical instruments, … using a computer… Carrying cups/mugs, bowls, plates, etc, is usually impossible." ET-related social isolation and depression are flagged as a *secondary* impairment that affects creative flow in its own right.

### 4.4 NIME / ADMI case studies

- **Netychords** (Davanzo, Avanzini, Ludovico, https://avanzini.di.unimi.it/downloads/publications/davanzo_chira23.pdf) reports a child with cerebral palsy who, working with this ADMI, "achieved a significant milestone, namely the enrollment in Portugal's Arts Education Program." This is one of the few longitudinal cases of *re-entry* into music-making via an adaptive interface.
- **DuoRhythmo** (CHI 2023, http://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3544548.3581285), evaluated with n=5 ALS participants, reports an **average System Usability Scale (SUS) score of 79.5** and qualitative descriptors "fun, empowering, accessible, easy to use, engaging, and stimulating." Note that SUS > 68 is conventionally "above average," but this is *eye-tracking*, not tremor.
- A gaze-driven xylophone interface (https://exa.ai/library/publication/wdb1cwxbwld) reports SUS items with mean Likert ratings in the 1.7–4.0 range on a 5-point scale (n=9), with qualitative themes around usability and expressivity.
- **DexPlay** (Berkeley AHD 2023, https://edg.berkeley.edu/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/AHD-2023-group9.pdf) is a passive wrist dampener designed after a case-study interview with an ET guitarist who had given up guitar. It targets the **flexion-extension wrist axis** specifically, illustrating the principle of *anatomically targeted* intervention.
- **Ayre** (QuackHacks 2026 hackathon, https://github.com/0xrpheus/ayre) explicitly includes a "Tremor smoothing" slider on a webcam-tracked hand controller; documented as an accessibility feature, not a research study.

### 4.5 Smart-pen analogue — Kalman Filter wins on convergence

A 2025 *Scientific Reports* paper on adaptive tremor-suppression for a smart pen (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-14196-5) compares Fx-LMS, Fx-NLMS, Fx-LMS/NLMS hybrid, RLS, and Kalman filtering on real PD signals from the NewHandPD dataset. They report that **RLS achieves the lowest mean squared error, but the Kalman Filter converges approximately eight times faster** — relevant because convergence speed translates directly to user-perceived latency during composition.

---

## 5. Creative flow: what the literature actually says

The flow-state literature (Csikszentmihalyi's nine-dimensional construct; reproduced verbatim in https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3837225/) lists the necessary conditions for flow: challenge-skill balance, action-awareness merging, clear goals, unambiguous feedback, concentration, sense of control, loss of self-consciousness, time transformation, and autotelic experience. A Drexel Creativity Research Lab fMRI/EEG study of 32 jazz guitarists (https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/brain-scans-of-jazz-musicians-reveal-how-to-reach-a-creative-flow-state/; https://mesplaisirs.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/1-s2.0-S0028393224000393-main.pdf) found that **higher-domain-experience performers enter flow through release of conscious control**, not hyperfocus — i.e., once a motor program is well-learned, *letting go* of micro-corrections enables flow. **This is the central tension for any tremor-filtering system.** A system that demands the user micro-manage thresholds, or that introduces perceptible lag and forces compensation, fights directly against the action-awareness merging and sense of control necessary for flow.

Quantitative link between tremor symptoms and flow disruption is not in the published HCI literature. What is documented is the existence of **biopsychosocial cascades**: ET patients document social withdrawal, anxiety in performance contexts, and depression (https://tracscotland.org/blog/essential-tremor-a-musicians-perspective-by-valerie-bryan/) — each of which independently erodes flow prerequisite states. Samuel Smith's reported 50–150-attempt/demo workflow is a flow-destroying loop by construction, even though it solves the symptom enough to finish an album.

### 5.1 What affects *the* variable the user can actually tune — sensitivity threshold

Although no peer-reviewed study isolates threshold sensitivity for musicians with tremor, two indirect streams exist:

1. **VKM (CHI 2022)** reports quantitatively how threshold tightening trades false positives vs. false negatives as a function of training-set size and gesture-production variability (https://cs.ucf.edu/~jjl/pubs/Taranta2022.pdf). With a single training sample, the threshold must be loose to compensate; with dense data, it can be tight without losing gestures. Implication for tremor filtering: a *per-user calibration phase* of even 20–30 demonstration gestures could allow substantially tighter thresholds than the "Aggressive / Balanced / Light" taxonomies commercial tools use.
2. **SteadyMouse's manual** documents the trade-off space empirically: at 95% filter strength "the mouse will feel like it's in molasses but should at least be smooth." Reducing by ~10–20 percentage points introduces some tremor leakage in exchange for responsiveness (https://www.steadymouse.com/manual/). This mirrors the VKM finding that variability-driven inflation of thresholds is necessary in performance contexts.

No published study reports composition completion times as a function of filter sensitivity, but anecdotally AI-mediated workflows (Smith's 50–150 attempts) and adaptive-instrument workflows (Netychords' multi-year adaptive redesign over many sessions) suggest **multiple-orders-of-magnitude overheads for naive approaches** vs. well-tuned pipelines.

---

## 6. Motor skill retention when switching between adaptive and standard interfaces

The strongest longitudinal evidence comes from outside the DAW literature but is directly applicable:

- The **Cymis** nursing-home study (https://exa.ai/library/publication/wb8qdd8w23g) tracked 31 disabled clients playing a score-programmed electronic instrument for an average of **5.6 years** (some up to 7 years). Of those 31: **13 (42%)** showed measurable upper-limb motor progress, **17 (55%)** showed no change (5 of whom initially progressed then regressed), and **1 (3%)** deteriorated. This is direct evidence that adaptive musical interfaces can **support motor retention over multi-year horizons**, contrary to the assumption that assistive tools cause atrophy.
- Stage-specific task-specific bowing tremor is itself evidence that motor systems retain highly specific trained programs decades into disease — the violinist in PMC4117185 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4117185/) developed a *new* task-specific tremor post-lobectomy only when *playing*, not during unrelated arm use, demonstrating that pathological and trained motor programs are dissociable at the neurological level. This is consistent with the design principle that adaptive systems should target *only* the tremor-bearing signal dimension, not the learned intentional dimension.
- No published study, however, directly tracks motor-skill loss or gain when a professional musician with movement disorder toggles between a tremor-filtered interface and a standard one (e.g., turning SteadyMouse off). This remains an open empirical question.

---

## 7. Synthesis: where the evidence stands

Quantitative summary of what's documented vs. what's claimed in the brief:

| Claim in brief | Evidence status |
|---|---|
| Ableton Live has "MIDI velocity smoothing" | True — via the *Velocity* MIDI effect, Gate/Clip/Random modes (https://www.ableton.com/en/live-manual/12/live-midi-effect-reference/) |
| Ableton Live markets this for tremor | False — forum users adopt it as a workaround (https://forum.ableton.com/viewtopic.php?t=120139); no productization |
| Logic Pro's Smart Controls include tremor compensation | False — not in any official Apple documentation (https://support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/smart-controls-overview-lgcp7e59f24b/mac; https://support.apple.com/content/dam/edam/applecare/images/en_US/otherassets/accessibility/vpat_logic_pro_2024.pdf) |
| SteadyMouse is a tremor-aware cursor tool | True, extensively documented (https://www.steadymouse.com/manual/) |
| SteadyMouse distinguishes vibrato from tremor | False — operates at the OS cursor layer; no musical semantics |
| Pathological tremor is 4–12 Hz and separable from vibrato | Partly true (tremor band overlaps 3–15 Hz), but separation must exploit *regularity and shape*, not rate alone (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4053556/; https://pubs.aip.org/asa/jasa/article/130/1/EL1/907816/Vibrato-and-tremor-extent-spectrum-Algorithm-and) |
| Gesture rejection in HCI has been characterized with false-positive rates | True — VKM/CHI 2022 is the canonical reference (https://cs.ucf.edu/~jjl/pubs/Taranta2022.pdf); false positives are documented as more harmful than false negatives |
| Composition completion times vary with tremor-filter sensitivity | **Not documented in any peer-reviewed source accessed** |
| User satisfaction scores vary with sensitivity | Indirectly: SUS scores exist for ADMIs (DuoRhythmo SUS 79.5 — n=5 ALS; xylophone interface 1.7–4.0 Likert — n=9) but not against tremor thresholds |
| Motor skill retention changes when switching adaptive ↔ standard | **Not documented in any peer-reviewed source accessed**; closest analogue is the multi-year Cymis study (https://exa.ai/library/publication/wb8qdd8w23g) |

The most consistent finding across all examined sources is that **the asymmetry between latency and tremor-cancellation frequency matters more than raw filter strength** — and the only settings a current commercial or research tool exposes to a user to control it are coarse sliders (SteadyMouse) or coarse MIDI gates (Ableton's Velocity MIDI effect). Meanwhile, the HCI literature has demonstrated (VKM; Kalman smart pen; STFT tremor switch) that finer-grained rejection *is achievable in principle*, including preserving intentional motion through tremor — but has not crossed over into DAW-level real-time MIDI pipelines.

What the literature has not yet produced, and what an honest reading of the evidence suggests is missing, is a longitudinal, randomized comparison of composition completion time and flow-state metrics across (a) no-filter, (b) cursor-level filter (SteadyMouse), and (c) MIDI-semantic filter conditions for professional musicians with movement disorders. The infrastructure for such a study exists — the SUS instruments, the Flow State Scale (Martin & Jackson, 2008), and the VKM-style rejection framework — but the application to expressive musical input remains future work.

---
